claims.text: The initial components have a coarse-grained boride coating prepared by conventional methods.
Oxidation at 750 °C for 15–30 minutes will form an Al2O3 surface layer on the boride coating.
Controlled slow cooling or chemical priming will enhance adhesion between the oxide and the boride coating.
The treatment will produce a thin Al2O3 layer.
The resulting Al2O3 layer will be continuous across the boride coating.
The resulting Al2O3 layer will be nanocrystalline.
The resulting Al2O3 layer will adhere strongly to the boride coating.
The pre-formed Al2O3 layer is chemically inert and thermally stable under molten-aluminum plating conditions.
The Al2O3 layer will act as a diffusion barrier that prevents direct interaction between molten aluminum and the underlying boride.
The adhesion-promoting step will prevent the Al2O3 barrier from spalling under thermal and mechanical stresses during plating.
Treated components will have lower molten-aluminum corrosion rates than untreated boride coatings.
Treated components will exhibit less aluminum penetration than untreated boride coatings.
Treated components will retain better coating integrity than untreated boride coatings.
The protective treatment will remain effective during exposure to molten aluminum at 660–700 °C in a controlled environment.
Extreme mechanical stress can compromise oxide-layer adhesion and protective effectiveness.
Deviations in oxygen control during treatment can compromise oxide-layer adhesion and protective effectiveness.
Formation of a protective Al2O3 barrier is well-supported.
